opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think it's becoming more relevant. For a long time the default mindset was that data is basically infinite: you scrape more of the web, you go bigger, and you never really see the same token twice. That world is slowly ending, at least for high-quality text, so people are being forced to think harder about getting more out of each token.

I think about it on a few levels.

First is the objective. Plain next-token prediction is great and very scalable, but it's not necessarily the most sample-efficient way to extract signal from a fixed corpus. That's part of why I've always been interested in mixing objectives: denoising, span corruption, prefix LM, the kind of mixture-of-denoisers idea. You're essentially looking at the same data through different lenses, and the model learns somewhat different things from each view. When you're data-constrained, that diversity of tasks over the same tokens can matter more.

Second is repetition. There's been good work showing you can repeat data for a few epochs without much degradation, and then returns fall off pretty sharply. So it's not that repetition is bad, it's that it has a budget. You want to be smart about what you repeat. Upweighting high-quality sources like code, math, and well-written text is usually a better use of that budget than uniformly cycling through everything.

Third is data quality and curation, which I think is still underrated relative to architecture tweaks. Deduplication, filtering, deciding the mixture: these are often where the biggest wins are, and they're not glamorous. A lot of what looks like a modeling breakthrough is honestly a data breakthrough.

And then there's synthetic data and distillation, which is the obvious frontier now. If you have a strong model, you can rephrase, augment, or generate data that's denser in useful signal. That works, but you have to be careful about collapse and about just amplifying the teacher's biases. It's a tool, not a free lunch.

The last thing I'd say is that architecture and scaling choices interact with all this. If you're data-constrained, the compute-optimal recipe shifts. You might want to spend compute differently, on more parameters, more epochs, or more inference-time compute, rather than following a scaling law fit in a data-rich regime. So I'd encourage people not to treat the old recipes as gospel. The constraint changes the optimal strategy, and you have to re-derive it empirically.

r001.rationale: In the data-constrained setting, the response recommends spending compute differently, including on more parameters or epochs, which communicates using more computation per training token to get more from limited data.

r002.rationale: It says the optimal recipe may differ from one fit in a data-rich regime, but does not state that scaling laws differ across learning algorithms.

r003.rationale: It mentions architecture and scaling choices interacting, but does not say an architectural improvement works by increasing computation per token.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, especially coming from the Google era where, honestly, data was never really the bottleneck. We had basically infinite web text, and the question was always compute. And then when you move to a smaller setting, or you're training for a specific domain, suddenly you realize that the Chinchilla-style scaling assumptions kind of break down because you just don't have twenty trillion clean tokens lying around.

So the first thing I'd say is, people underestimate how much mileage you can get from multiple epochs. There was this kind of folk belief for a while that you should never repeat data, that it's always better to see a fresh token. And I think that's just not true. The Muennighoff et al. work showed this pretty clearly, that you can go to something like four epochs with almost no degradation relative to fresh data, and even beyond that the returns decay gracefully rather than falling off a cliff. So if you're data constrained, the first lever is actually just, train longer on what you have. It sounds dumb but a lot of people don't do it.

The second thing is quality over quantity, which everyone says now, but I want to be a bit more precise about it. I think the real insight is that the marginal token matters a lot more than people think. If you have a fixed data budget, aggressive filtering, deduplication, and especially near-dedup, give you more effective tokens than the raw count suggests. And the flip side is that low-quality data isn't neutral, it actually costs you. It's not just wasted compute, it can actively hurt the model.

Then there's the architecture and objective side, which is kind of my background. The denoising objectives we did with UL2 were partly motivated by this. If you think about it, a pure causal LM gets one gradient signal per token, basically next-token prediction. But with mixture-of-denoisers, you're extracting multiple different learning signals from the same underlying text, span corruption, prefix LM, and so on. So in a sense you're getting more supervision per byte of data. I don't think that's a silver bullet, but when data is the constraint rather than compute, I think objective design becomes a lot more interesting again. It kind of went out of fashion because at scale, causal decoders just win on simplicity, but in the constrained regime the calculus changes.

And the last thing, which is maybe the most important practically, is synthetic data, but done carefully. I'm somewhat skeptical of the naive version where you just have a big model generate a bunch of stuff and train on it, because you inherit all the biases and you can get this kind of collapse. But rephrasing, augmentation, generating diverse views of existing high-quality data, that genuinely works. You're basically using compute to manufacture data diversity, which is exactly the trade you want to make when compute is cheaper than data for you.

So I guess if I had to summarize: repeat your data more than you think, filter harder than you think, reconsider the training objective, and use compute to create data. Those are the four levers.

r001.rationale: It recommends training for more epochs on the available data, explicitly using additional training to get more mileage from each available token.

r002.rationale: It says Chinchilla-style assumptions break down in data-constrained settings and that the objective-design calculus changes, but does not state that scaling laws differ across learning algorithms.

r003.rationale: It describes mixture-of-denoisers as extracting multiple learning signals from the same text, but does not say the architectural improvement works by increasing computation per token.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: how much learning are you getting out of each token? We often focus on the number of tokens, but the training objective and the quality of the data matter a lot, especially when you can’t just collect more.

One direction is to get richer learning signals from the same examples. You can expose the model to different prediction tasks or different ways of masking the input, so that revisiting an example isn’t necessarily repeating exactly the same learning problem. Of course, you still have to measure whether that helps generalization.

Then there’s data selection. More data isn’t always more useful data. If your budget is constrained, you want examples that contribute something the model hasn’t already learned. Synthetic data can help, but I wouldn’t equate generating more tokens with creating more information. The question is whether those tokens provide useful variation or a better training signal.

So I’d think about the data, the objective, and the model together, rather than treating data efficiency as just a filtering problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses richer learning signals and objectives, but does not identify spending more computation per training token as a way to improve data efficiency.

r002.rationale: It does not mention scaling laws or state that they can differ across learning algorithms.

r003.rationale: It does not describe an architectural improvement or connect one to increased computation per token.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate two things: getting more signal out of the data you already have, and finding ways to create additional useful signal. If data is the bottleneck, just making the model bigger or training longer may not be the best use of compute.

For the first part, I would look at the training objective, the quality of the data, and how you sample it. Are you spending a lot of compute on examples that are redundant or that the model already handles well? Can you formulate the learning problem so each example teaches the model more? Those choices can matter as much as the architecture.

Then there’s synthetic data, but the important thing is whether it adds something. Generating more text doesn’t automatically give you more information. You want diversity, useful supervision, and ideally some way to verify the outputs. Otherwise, you can just amplify the same mistakes.

So I’d think about data efficiency as a property of the whole training recipe. The question is: for a fixed amount of real data and a fixed compute budget, how much useful learning can you extract?
